review: This Near West Side donut shop is part of a Hawaiian-based chain with locations across the country. And though chains are usually hit-or-miss, their mochi donuts are great. Mochinut’s rice flour base means they have a stretchy, sticky interior and a crispy exterior. There are over 20 to choose from, but the savory and fruity flavors complement the dough more than the straight-up sweet ones. So go for the black sesame, matcha, or mango.
perfect_for_tags: Dessert, Pastries, Coffee & A Light Bite, Serious Take-Out Operation, Bakery/Cafe, Dessert

review: At Mini Donut Factory, it's possible to try six different donuts, without suffering from the side effects of eating six donuts in a short period of time. And that's because every donut at this Lakeview spot is tiny. They come in orders of six, which essentially adds up to one regular-sized donut. Each one is soft and tastes like funnel cake, and all of the toppings are added when you order. The raspberry has just enough tartness and the cookies and cream taste like a fried Oreo.
perfect_for_tags: Bakery/Cafe

review: Honey's used to be in Bucktown, but relocated to Bronzeville in 2015. The menu is the same, which means hickory-smoked ribs and tips, pulled pork, wings, and fish. The sauce has enough honey flavor to make you understand the origins of this counter-service spot's name, giving everything a sweet, smoky taste. Just know it's cash-only, but there's an ATM inside the restaurant.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, BBQ

review: If you still haven’t had BBQ from The Slab in South Shore, now is the perfect time to correct this. The specialty here are St. Louis-style ribs, which have a satisfyingly charred bark lacquered with a sweet and slightly spicy Chicago sauce. All the sides are made from scratch, and must-orders are the mac and cheese, candied, yams, and baked beans.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, BBQ

review: Located in the Richland Center food court in Chinatown, J's Snack Shop is one of the best reasons to eat in a basement. And that’s because this food stall's potato noodle soup is fantastic. The spicy broth is savory with lots of flavor from the different ingredients floating around—vegetables, tofu, fish balls, and quail eggs. But it's the thick and squishy potato noodles that really ties everything together.
perfect_for_tags: Quick Eats, Dining Solo, Lunch, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Chinese

review: Depending on where you look and who you ask, this spot might be known as A Place In Northeast or A Family In Northeast. But, despite any confusion about the name of this Chinese stall in the Richland Center food court, they have great sheng jian bao and jiang bing. The beef buns have a peppery filling with a thick wrapper with a crispy bottom. The beef jiang bing is equally tasty—the pancake is light and flaky, and the thin slices of beef are covered in a sweet and spicy sauce.
perfect_for_tags: Quick Eats, Dining Solo, Lunch, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Chinese

review: Ma Gong La Po used to have its own storefront above ground, but has since moved into a food stall at the Richland Center food court in Chinatown. But despite downsizing, the menu is still fairly long and full of tasty dishes. The dumplings (like xiao long bao or pickled cabbage pork) are pretty good, but definitely get the lamb skewers. Each order comes with four and the meat has plenty of smoky cumin.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Quick Eats, Lunch, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Chinese

review: For a quick bowl of rice or noodles, Fresh Fast Food in Chinatown's Richland Center has you covered. This food stall has plenty of noodle dishes to choose from, like saucy shredded pork or a comforting bowl of beef rice noodle soup. And though they have many varieties of fried rice, focus on the steamed rice bowls. They come with everything from soy sauce-braised pork trotters to stir-fried tomatoes and eggs.
perfect_for_tags: Quick Eats, Dining Solo, Lunch, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Chinese

review: Kylin Teppanyaki is a veteran stall at Chinatown's Richland Center food court, and it seems like it's been making Japanese food since before the Columbian Exposition. The long menu has lighter dishes like crispy okonomiyaki and takoyaki, along with heartier options like curry katsu bento boxes and bowls of udon.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Lunch, Dining Solo, Quick Eats, Japanese, Chinese

review: The counter at this Richland Center food stall is covered with metal containers filled with different cuts of pre-cooked meat. Pork, chicken, duck, beef—you can find it all at Jue Wei Ya Ba Wang in Chinatown. The person working will scoop up some duck necks, pig ears, or beef tendons, chop them up, toss them in chili sauce, or brush on a sweet and savory glaze. While the sauces are pretty tasty, we do wish that the meat was heated up before serving.
perfect_for_tags: Quick Eats, Dining Solo, Lunch, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Chinese

review: You can walk around Wentworth, Cermak, and Chinatown Square and never find Elite Boba. That's because this great bubble tea spot is actually located underground, in the Richland Center's basement food court. This tea shop has a massive selection of milk tea, fruit smoothies, and fruit tea, all of which can be customized. You can be as detailed as you want, picking sugar levels, the amount of ice, and choosing toppings ranging from tapioca to Oreo cheese foam.
perfect_for_tags: Chinese

review: Umamicue is a Vietnamese-Chinese-American BBQ pop-up at Spilt Milk in Logan Square. They also have some of the best brisket in Chicago. By itself, in an eggroll, in a banh mi—the buttery meat is great in any form. The short menu also has tangy chuc nuam-infused potato salad, smoked cream cheese crab rangoon, and pork belly with distinct layers of fat, meat, and crackly skin. Pair everything with a cocktail, and sit out on the spacious back patio.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Dining Solo, Eating At The Bar, Walk-Ins, Vietnamese, BBQ

review: Pop’s is a primarily suburban chain throughout Illinois and Indiana that serves Italian beef, burgers, hot dogs, and other fast food items. They tout “the art of a beef sandwich,” with signs around the store highlighting the ways you can customize your order. And they truly differentiate between levels of soppiness here. You’ll want to get your sandwich wet, or at least dipped, because the bread (like the beef) is quite tough. The meat is chewy, and the overarching flavor is “salt”, which isn’t helped by the massive pile of giardiniera on top. The lone Chicago location of Pop’s doesn’t have any seating, though there is standing-only counter space and a patio out front. While a dry sandwich is manageable to eat indoors, the outdoor tables are a good call so you can comfortably make a mess as you try to wrangle your wet Italian beef.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, American, Burgers

review: Want an Italian beef with a side of kitschy decor? Look no further than Luke’s, a counter-service spot in the Loop seemingly plucked from one of Universal Studios' themed city-scapes. However, the massive Italian beef sculpture protruding from the wall looks more appealing than the real version actually is. Sure, the bread doesn’t disintegrate under the weight of the beef, but that’s because the beef is kind of dry and stringy. The meat has no flavor, as though it was boiled in unspiced gravy. Luke’s is filled with unsuspecting tourists eating close to their hotel, or people working in the neighborhood who have exactly 12 minutes between meetings to grab lunch—and they’re probably ordering one of the other sandwiches, pastas, or pizza slices on the menu instead.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, American, Italian

review: Patio Restaurant in Little Italy is known for its Italian beef. But this cash-only, counter-service spot has a different definition of what makes a good Italian beef compared to the many other fine establishments in (and outside of) Chicago. The beef is sliced thick, and it’s dry and tough. Every bite feels like an eternity, and no amount of dipping or peppers helps the situation. There are other things to try on the menu (like the usual sausages and hot dogs) but we suggest visiting Al’s or Carm’s (both of which are nearby) for a great Italian beef instead.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, American, Fast Food

review: Mr. Beef & Pizza is a pizzeria and sandwich shop in Dunning. Pizza seems to take precedence here, and it’s telling that Italian beef is nowhere to be found under the “Our Most Popular Items” section of the website. The bread is tasty (but disintegrates easily even when just slightly dipped), and they’re not shy about the amount of pepper topping. But the sandwich tastes overwhelmingly of oil and Italian seasoning, which doesn’t counterbalance the unpleasant iron-y flavor of the meat. Head to nearby Bob-O's instead for a better Italian beef.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Pizza

review: All neighborhoods should have a Chengdu Impression. But until this casual Sichuan spot truly initiates a Chicago takeover, you can only find them in Lincoln Park, Wicker Park, and this corner location in Edgewater. This particular one is the largest and least busy, making it great for taking a bunch of friends out for some delicious spicy Chinese food. Wontons in chili sauce and chewy dandan noodles are a must, and don't bother trying to decide between dry chili chicken or tart and spicy stewed rabbit—just get both.
perfect_for_tags: Big Groups, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Chinese

review: Unfortunately, the Red Line won't bring you directly to Falafel Kebab Station, but considering that it is right next to the Granville stop, we'll take it. And the reason we want a direct route to this counter-service Mediterranean spot is because the food is great. Whether it’s a perfectly griddled lemony chicken shawarma wrap or a giant rice plate with beef, lamb, and chicken kabobs, the menu is full of hits. Plus, the food comes out quickly and there are lots of booths and high tables.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Quick Eats, Dining Solo, Walk-Ins, Mediterranean

review: This barstaurant feels a little bit like an upstate NY traveler's lodge, complete with a cozy brick space, a long bar, and dark wooden accents. There are also positive affirmations that a restaurant would say to itself in the mirror sprinkled around. But we can confirm that Beard and Belly does, in fact, have “good food” and “fun times.” The crowd of longtime Edgewater residents and temporary Loyola students creates a busy, friendly atmosphere that’s welcoming for everyone. And after eating beer-battered pickles, chicken pot pie hand pies, and a burger with creamy Butterkäse, you might start whispering generic positive sayings, too.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Drinking Good Beer, Drinks & A Light Bite, Eating At The Bar, Dining Solo, Walk-Ins, Gastropub

review: This casual Serbian restaurant is an incredible one-woman show. The chef-owner takes orders, busses tables, grills up cevapi—and somehow still finds time to frequently check in on you. And while the cevapi is great, there lots of other delicious dishes, from big bowls of stuffed cabbage and mashed potatoes, to flaky spinach and cheese burek. The diner-esque space with old-school tables and booths is pretty sparse (other than a TV playing infomercials). But you won’t care about the undecorated space when you’re preoccupied with more important things, like dipping housemade bread in rich bean stew.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Walk-Ins, Serious Take-Out Operation, European, Serbian

review: With a consistent stream of regulars and a retro diner look full of Naugahyde booths, this corner restaurant lives up to its name. But more importantly, their long menu has all the diner food classics. Eggs, crispy hash browns, fluffy pancakes—it’s all here and it’s all tasty. Lunch-ish things like chicken wraps or their cheeseburger are solid, too. The bright interior has plenty of seating, but be sure to get there early on the weekends because it’s always packed.
perfect_for_tags: Breakfast, Lunch, Walk-Ins, Brunch, Diner, Breakfast

review: Sweet Mandy B’s in Lincoln Park is our go-to sweet shop whenever we, as adults, want to eat a chocolate dirt cup topped with gummy worms, or rice krispy treats topped with frosting and sprinkles. But they also have options that don’t sound like something you begged your mom to have at your eighth birthday party—like key lime pie, scones, and flourless chocolate cake. That said, you should still order her a Double Doozie—a chocolate chip cookie sandwich stuffed with edible cookie dough.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, Kids, Bakery/Cafe

review: The food at this casual BYOB spot in Logan Square is hit-or-miss, but since the Spice Room’s long menu doesn’t change, you don’t need to worry about them getting rid of the hits. Some things, like the chicken chettinad or gobi manchurian are appropriately spicy with the right balance of chili and vinegar. Others, like the butter chicken and bhindi masala, are flavorless or too oily. But most dishes end up snatching defeat from the jaws of culinary victory. The samosas come with a crispy dough that’s wonderfully light and flaky, but the potato and pea filling is bland. Similarly, the chicken tikka and malai tikka taste good but are too dry, the tandoori chicken is tender but lacks the expected smoky flavor, and the dal makhani is hearty but way too salty. All that being said, you won’t have a truly bad meal here, and the flaws are tempered by the friendly service and warm atmosphere.
perfect_for_tags: BYOB, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Delivery, Vegetarians, Indian

review: Uri-Swati is a solid option for vegetarian food on Devon when there aren’t any tables available at Annapurna. Get your fix of South Indian dishes like soft-in-the-middle and crispy-on-the-outside uttapam, or the impossibly thin Mysore masala dosa that comes with a delicious and fresh coconut chutney. Or, enjoy a paratha meal that comes with a tasty lassuni dal while catching up on the latest Bollywood music videos playing in Uru-Swati’s dining room. But skip the idli (too dry and hard) and overcooked vada which is bordering on burned.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Vegans, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Indian, Vegetarian

review: This vegetarian spot’s specialty is dosa, which makes up a significant portion of the long menu. Udupi Palace’s versions of the South Indian dish have well-crisped edges, but taste over-fermented, and are served with a perfectly acceptable (if too salty) sambar. You’ll find plain dosas, ones filled with potatoes and onions or chutney and cheese, and varieties made with lentil flour instead of rice. The idlis are slightly better, and if you go early in the day (say, during lunch by yourself), you’ll likely get them with sambar that’s tangy and doesn’t taste too reduced. The restaurant is quiet, and ideal for a low-key dinner with friends or a weeknight dinner alone, but we suggest visiting Annapurna for a great vegetarian meal on Devon instead.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Indian, Vegetarian

review: There are plenty of things to keep you distracted at this 20-year-old River North restaurant. No less than nine different types of light fixtures (including two different styles of chandeliers with only half the bulbs installed, and an LED light that changes colors every 30 seconds), tables with built-in fire features, and a menu filled with questionable names for Indo-Chinese dishes like “Crazy Hot Asians,” “What’s Your Beef,” and desserts simply named “Sex.” But all of the attempts at being edgy can't distract from the fact that the food at Vermilion is mediocre. Like the tangra chaat, which tastes like it was tossed in bottled masala ketchup. Or a plate of hakka noodles that’s essentially just a warm, soggy version of the chaat. The cocktails, however, are tasty. So if you find yourself at Vermilion because your out-of-town colleagues planned the team offsite dinner, just order a few “Bollywood Item Numbers” or mango mint mojitos, and spend the rest of the evening trying to figure out how to change those bulbs.
perfect_for_tags: Wasting Your Time and Money, Indian

review: Luzzat, a small, casual spot underneath the Jarvis Red Line stop in Rogers Park, focuses on food from North India. And this place doesn’t have naan on the menu—we repeat, doesn’t have naan. But that’s not the only drawback: Most of the dishes here taste like they’ve been reheated after a six month stint in the deep freezer. While the portions are large, you likely won’t want to save your leftovers.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Indian

review: If you’re not already someone who dreams about eating lamb seekh kabob so tender that it melts in your mouth, a visit to Bundoo Khan in Rogers Park will change that. This fantastic Pakistani restaurant also serves the best biryani in the city, the juiciest chicken malai boti we’ve ever had, and special rolls stuffed with beef or chicken wrapped in naan so soft and fluffy we’d like to take a nap under it.  The rest of the menu is made up of karahi and grilled meats, which is what you’ll find on most of the tables in the large dining room, filled with families and small groups of locals. Bundoo Khan is probably not where you want to bring your vegetarian roommate (there are exactly three vegetarian options on the menu, besides rice and paratha). But your cousin who fancies themselves a grill master will appreciate the massive operation right at the entrance, complete with whole raw chickens being skewered and barbecued to perfection.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Walk-Ins, Pakistani

review: Like its sister location in the South Loop, Nepal House on Devon Avenue is a small sit-down restaurant serving Nepali and Indian food. We like this location a little more because the food is just as good (if not better) and it’s relatively mellow on weeknights. The menu has everything from Nepali BBQ to better-than-average North Indian staples—and you should opt for an order of not-too-doughy samosas and a plate of momos. There aren’t that many tables in the narrow dining room, but there are a few small booths that are perfect for a lone diner to settle in with a beer, a piping hot curry, and a basket of pillowy-soft garlic naan.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Dining Solo, Serious Take-Out Operation, Vegetarians, Nepali, Indian

review: Mild 2 Spicy in Lakeview is the perfect spot for when you want to zone out while eating Indian food. This casual restaurant is painted black and dotted with wood accents and greenery, giving the large dining room an industrial yet calm vibe. That means you can turn your attention to the very tasty Mysore masala dosa—it’s crispy and paper-thin, layered with an appropriately spicy chutney. Apart from the inexplicably long dosa section, the rest of the menu is mostly North Indian dishes with a lot of vegetarian options (most of which can be made vegan). In fact, the non-vegetarian dishes are fine, but Mild 2 Spicy really shines with things like aloo gobi masala or channa saag, where there’s not a single piece of overcooked chicken breast in sight.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Delivery, Lunch, Serious Take-Out Operation, Vegans, Vegetarians, Indian

review: Visit Tandoor Char House when you want a slightly more upscale experience than what you’ll get at nearby Mild 2 Spicy. This Lincoln Park spot is elevated both figuratively and literally—from the need for reservations, attentive service, and heavy black tablecloths to the fact that the small dining room is actually elevated—with only eight tables overlooking the entrance of the restaurant. There’s a long menu of classic Pakistani and North Indian dishes (mostly tandoor entrees and karahi) done well, but the most interesting things to try are the specialty fusion dishes, like the tandoor chicken empanada, tamarind wings, and tikka masala tacos.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Quiet Meals, Pakistani, Indian

review: Half-Indian cafe, half-dessert shop, Sukhadia is a Chicago institution that’s perfect for a light bite and  cup of chai. This casual counter-service spot has been the go-to snack shop on Devon since 1995, and the weekend crowds are a testament to how popular Sukhadia still is. The dining room doesn’t have much in the way of ambiance (it’s loud, sometimes chaotic, and there’s a good chance your table will be sticky when you sit down), but you won’t care once you get your hands on some vada pav and papdi chaat. Round out your snack-turned-meal with dessert—we especially like the cham cham, but really any of the 9,372,505 options in the glass case up front will do.
perfect_for_tags: Coffee & A Light Bite, Quick Eats, Indian, Dessert

review: Johnnie's Beef in Elmwood Park knows exactly what it’s doing when it comes to Italian beef. Not just because the sandwiches are great—which they are—but because this cash-only spot is a well-oiled Italian beef-making machine. The stand has been serving perfectly seasoned beef swimming in a delightfully salty gravy since 1961, and it’s a study in efficiency. There are no less than five people behind the counter, making sure you’ll have your sandwich, fries, and Italian ice within 30-seconds from placing your order. So don’t be discouraged if you see a line (which you will) because it moves quickly.
perfect_for_tags: Cheap Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, Classic Establishment, Sandwiches
full_address: 7500 W North Ave, Elmwood Park, IL 60707

review: It doesn’t matter if you’re dining solo at the bar, with a date admiring the cute horsies on the banquette, or keeping the peace at a twelve-seat round table—you’re at this Humboldt Park spot for the fried chicken. It has the perfect crispy-to-juicy ratio, and comes with rich gravy, fluffy biscuits, and chile-maple butter. But the new American menu has a few other things worth trying, like the crab gravy with rice, or their pillowy baked potato gnocchi. Make sure to also check out Split Rail’s basement speakeasy, Dorothy (which has excellent cocktails), and their art gallery next door, The Martin.
food_rundown:
Chips And Dip

This appetizer sounds very simple, and on a superficial level, it is. But the super-thin housemade chips are expertly salted and fried, and the french onion dip is fresh and flavorful. It’s served with a side of trout roe, a.k.a. rec room caviar.


Chicken Nuggets

Like the kind you’d get in a Happy Meal - except these taste like they’re made from real meat. It kind of freaked us out how much we liked them.


Loaded Baked Potato Gnocchi

Gnocchi turns out to be a perfect vehicle for loaded potato toppings - which makes sense, when you think about it.


Toast # 2

This is topped with fig jam, brussels sprouts, and fried oysters, and it’s very bad. The sweetness of the jam and the funkiness of the brussels sprouts don’t go well with the oysters at all, and somehow the fact that the bread itself tastes good makes the overall dish worse.


Wild Boar Bolognese

The sauce on this tastes like it was seasoned with a Hamburger Helper spice packet. That might make it sound terrible, but clearly Split Rail has a team of scientists figuring out what makes that stuff good without being gross.


Spiced Pork And Beef Meatballs

We can’t decide if these are actually supposed to taste like meatloaf and gravy, or if the rest of the retro dishes on the menu just create that perception. The meatballs are tender and flavorful, and get an upgrade with a pumpkin romesco sauce. It’s a great dish.


Lamb Tartare 

This doesn’t really go with the theme, so we figure it’s only on the menu for one reason - someone here can make a great lamb tartare. Order it.


Roasted Vegetable Medley

Broccoli is the primary ingredient in this medley, which comes with a white cheddar cheese sauce. It’s not exactly diet food, and it reminds us of a frozen Green Giant broccoli and cheese steam bag, in a bad way. It’s too heavy and doesn’t have much flavor except salt.


Fajitas, Reimagined

This sounds more like an Onion headline than something we want to eat, but the steak is cooked perfectly, it’s seasoned like fajitas, and the corn puree (a reimagined tortilla, we guess) and red pepper gelee on the plate are really good.


A Duck In Three Acts

As you might guess based on the name, this dish has duck three ways: a roasted breast, a duck egg, and a duck leg scrumpet (that’s pressed, rolled in breadcrumbs, and fried). It’s a take on a chicken and rice dinner, and all three versions of the duck taste good, but the parsnips on the side just make us want potatoes.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Date Night, Eating At The Bar, Small Plates, American, Bar Food

review: Don’t underestimate this small Edgewater ramen shop next to the Thorndale Red Line—despite its size, Kohoku-ku Ramen has personality. The colorful dining room is decked out in vibrant koi kites, empty sake barrels, and little curtains hanging from private booths that are perfect if you feel self-conscious about your noodle-slurping face. Their straightforward shoyu and tonkatsu bowls are great, but if you want a unique bowl, the spicy specialty ramen with soft shell crab and fried shrimp is good, too. Kohoku-ku isn’t usually too busy, so it’s perfect for a relaxed dinner after a long day and/or a ride on the L.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Walk-Ins, Ramen

review: Pizza Matta comes from the team behind Giant, it’s fantastic next-door neighbor in Logan Square that’s one of The Best Restaurants In Chicago. But this take-out-only pizza place is disappointing. The pies are all build-your-own, so you can go as unhinged as you want. But even if you’ve engineered the perfect topping combination, you'll end up with a boring pizza. The bland dough is straight down the middle—neither thick nor thin—but less of a Goldilocks perfect medium and more of a “well, I guess this works.” The sauce and cheese are also unengaging, lacking flavor and zestiness. There are too many good pizza places in Chicago for just-fine, so if you’re in the area and want a good pie, make your way to Middle Brow or Paulie Gee’s.
perfect_for_tags: Pizza

review: Housemade pasta, good wine, and a dimly lit space that’s cozy enough for a date but large enough for a birthday—Il Milanese has all the makings of a great neighborhood restaurant. But in reality, this North Center Italian spot ends up feeling more like a place you settle on rather than a go-to spot. The housemade pastas (like pappardelle and duck-filled ravioli) have a great texture. But a snoozy tomato sauce or too-rich porcini cream sauce both end up overshadowing the pasta. Other dishes fumble at the one-yard line too, like a perfectly cooked osso bucco that comes with salty risotto. But while the food misses the target, the long bar makes it a great spot to hang out for a glass of wine—especially if you’re waiting for a seat at the busy (and fantastic) ramen spot next door, Menya Goku.
perfect_for_tags: Drinking Good Wine, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Date Night, Italian

review: With only three tables, R. Haan Thai is, for all intents and purposes, a very small restaurant. But since most people are just coming in for take-out, you never need to worry about finding a spot to sit. The food here is solid, with some satisfying curries and noodle dishes, but the best dishes are actually the starters. The larb kai has a balanced combination of lime and fish sauce, the tom kha has plenty of lemongrass, and the deep-fried pork belly is perfectly crispy. There isn’t much in terms of ambiance aside from a few vintage knick-knacks, but if you happen to be in the area, it’s a good option for a casual meal.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Walk-Ins, Thai

review: Pigtail is a pig-themed cocktail bar underneath Jaleo in River North. And if you somehow didn’t get the theme after seeing the big glowing sign that says “Pig and Cocktail” at the back wall, there’s no shortage of reminders. Sleek booths have funny portraits of pigs in powdered wigs overlooking them, small winged pig figurines decorate the walls, and the most prominent ingredient on the menu is pork.  But while the theme is consistent, the food isn’t. Croquettes topped with thin slivers of iberico ham are fantastic, but an iberico smashburger topped with cheese espuma ends up tasting too rich and salty. The drinks are actually quite good—as long as you order straightforward ones like the bourbon-based Black Hole Sun and avoid the experimental ones, like an imbalanced and confusing boozy consome cocktail with pork bone broth, egg foam, and amontillado.
perfect_for_tags: Drinks & A Light Bite, Drinking Good Cocktails, Date Night, Walk-Ins, Spanish, Bar

review: This two-story spot is part retail shop and part wine bar. The first floor is like a tiny library, with shelves stocked top to bottom with bottles. The second floor is where you’ll find the much more spacious bar—full of high tables, wooden booths, and occasionally, live music or a restaurant pop-up. They also happen to have great happy hour deals where a glass or a cocktail only costs $8.
perfect_for_tags: Big Groups, Drinking Good Wine, Outdoor/Patio Situation, Wine Bar

review: Rainbow Thai is a casual neighborhood spot in Lincoln Square that’s useful for takeout and delivery. The online delivery menu is much longer than the dine-in one, meaning it has curries and fried rice along with various noodle dishes and entrees. Whatever you order will likely feature wonderfully crunchy vegetables, a warming heat, and mellow flavors—like the cashew chicken (which is great), “crazy spicy” noodles (which aren't particularly crazy or spicy), or a too-sweet pad thai that tastes like it was cooked in apple cider. The small dining area has a few tables, but it's usually easy enough to get a seat when you really can’t stand the thought of eating another dinner on your couch.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Delivery, Serious Take-Out Operation, Thai

review: Come to Thai Pastry to eat Thai food in a space that feels like a cross between a college campus café and your friend’s basement rec room. The carpeted, cozy Uptown space is surrounded by seasonal decor like jack-o-lanterns (in May), grocery shelves lined with snacks, a dessert display case, and a TV playing travel shows with Thai subtitles. The dishes are solid, from the curry fried rice to pad khee mao, and the pumpkin and eggplant curry—but stick to the Thai dishes here and pass on things like sweet and sour chicken. They’ll also make most of the menu without eggs, fish or oyster sauce, so it’s a great spot for vegetarians and vegans.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Vegetarians, Thai

review: This Southern restaurant is hidden on the ground floor of an apartment complex behind the Wrigley Building. Once you find the entrance (which shouldn’t be hard since the door is surrounded by the wedding industrial complex’s entire flower inventory), you’re in for a dinner filled with just-fine drinks and middling food like the short rib-in-the-style-of-hamburger-helper or fried catfish with too much breading. But mostly, you’ll be treated to the space's “ode to Southern charm” theme, which in this case means being decorated like a sorority social chair’s Bid Day Bash nightmare—complete with pink velvet seating, white marble tables, gold accents, flowers throughout, and a lone tumbleweed rolling through the empty dining room. The front of the restaurant is a little more lively, with a bar and loud music, so it works for a quick drink and a plate of fried pickles before going somewhere else in River North.
perfect_for_tags: Drinks & A Light Bite, Southern

review: Pochos describes itself as “your friendly neighborhood brunch restaurant” and that’s exactly what it is. The menu at this Mexican cafe in Pilsen is mostly made up of sweet and savory brunch dishes, like caramel french toast or chorizo eggs benedict, plus sandwiches—including a tasty Cuban sandwich with pickled mustard seed aioli that we’d be happy to eat at 10am or 4pm (when Pochos closes). During the week, it’s the kind of cozy yet fun place you want to stay and hang, with colorful decor and upbeat music played at a volume that’s still a vibe but doesn’t force you to yell across the table. But Pochos is extremely busy on the weekends, so expect a long wait if you visit at prime brunch time.
perfect_for_tags: Breakfast, Brunch, Lunch, Breakfast, Mexican

review: Taylor’s Tacos has a familiar origin story: it began as a pop-up, moved operations to a shared kitchen, and finally graduated to a brick-and-mortar of its own. What isn’t so familiar? It’s Chicago’s first Black-owned, female-owned, queer-owned taco shop. This counter-service spot feels airy, with soft peach, pink, and wood tones, and large windows that flood the small space with light. They have a short menu of tacos with fillings like chicken, steak, shrimp, sweet potato, and a weekly special like fish or asparagus. The tacos are small but stuffed, so you’ll definitely be able to make use of the double-stacked tortillas (which happen to be delicious, despite being a little greasy). Our favorite is the sweet potato—crispy on the outside, soft on the inside, and perfectly balanced with salsa, cilantro, hot sauce, and pickled red cabbage. Keep in mind there are only five tables, and its proximity to the Medical District means that if you visit during lunch you should be prepared to get your order to go.
perfect_for_tags: Lunch, Serious Take-Out Operation, Vegetarians, Mexican, Tacos

review: Nobus are ubiquitous in major cities, and Chicago’s very own is in the West Loop, at the bottom of the (you guessed it) Nobu Hotel. It has an identical Japanese fusion menu to its brethren, with dishes like miso cod, tuna crispy rice, and black truffle ribeye. Some are better than others, but nothing is mindblowing. What is mindblowing is how expensive the bill will be—especially for just-fine food and an unpredictable dining experience that might have you surrounded by tables filled with sulking couples, MMA fighters on their phones, recent grads celebrating with the parents, and an ever-growing pile of dirty dishes the staff is too busy to clear. Instead of coming here for dinner, head to the elevators and go up to the much-more-fun rooftop bar. There you get a lovely view, and don’t have to order any food.
perfect_for_tags: See And Be Seen, People Watching, Japanese, Fusion

review: Legend has it that Al’s invented the original Italian beef in 1938, and while that legend might have been started by Al’s, it’s still a perfect sandwich. It will come on fluffy bread packed with slices of beef marinated in more than just the usual pepper and garlic. The secret spice recipe is definitely hidden in a tungsten safe, and probably surrounded by a moat of their bright orange jus. Order a cup of this liquid gold (a must for dunking), so you can control the structural integrity of your sandwich. Don’t bother with the other locations—go to the one on Taylor Street. That’s where they marinate and roast their beef, and we believe in getting Al’s straight from the source.
perfect_for_tags: Classic Establishment, Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Fast Food

review: When you’re standing in line debating on what to order and hear “doesn’t matter, this is the best Italian beef in Chicago” from the guy behind you, it’s a good sign. That’s what happened to us the first time we went to Tony's. And we’re happy to report that, while prone to hyperbole, he wasn’t a liar. The sandwich at Tony’s, a south side staple in West Lawn, has perfectly spiced beef topped with tender sweet peppers, and it’s good enough on its own, even if you order it dry. But skip the giardiniera, this sandwich doesn’t need it.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Fast Food

review: Buona has all the hallmarks of a chain restaurant—ordering kiosks, lots of metal seating, big screen TVs—but at the Streeterville location (which is the only outpost in Chicago) that’s not a bad thing. For one, they'll let you customize your Italian beef in a bunch of ways, including offering plant-based options. Plus it’s always consistent. The beef at Buona is sliced so thin it’s beyond the scope of man’s physical abilities, and each individual slice is packed with meaty, umami flavor and a pleasant black peppery-ness. The filling is juicy enough on its own (and topped with an exorbitant amount of giardiniera) that it doesn’t need to be ordered wet, but if you do decide to get it “baptized” (Buona’s term of choice), the bread will hold up well.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Fast Food

review: Carm’s is on a quiet corner in University Village, just a few blocks away from the traffic on Taylor Street. You’ll find plenty of things on the menu, but the main attraction at this small shop is the Italian beef. Not only is the side of jus here the best in Chicago—more like a peppery consommé—but the bread is so flavorful that you can even order the sandwich dry. The correct move, though, is to get your order dipped, and follow it up with a refreshing Italian ice as a palette cleanser from the separate, cash-only dessert counter.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Fast Food

review: This small family-run operation in Portage Park has been around since 1968, and they’ve used the past 55 years to perfect the bread-to-meat ratio of their excellent Italian beef. At Roma’s, sandwiches come on bread that’s downright Cancerian: secretly tender, with a tough exterior capable of withstanding a dip (which is how you should order it). Add in the thin slices of mildly flavored beef, plus gentle heat from the hot peppers, and the result is a surprisingly light Italian beef. Conveniently, you can also get Roma’s sandwiches in half-sizes to keep things even lighter. Inconveniently, they only take cash (or Venmo or Zelle).
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, American, Fast Food

review: Southtown Sub is a small, take-out-only sandwich shop in Greater Grand Crossing that’s best known for its classic Chicago sandwich, the Gym Shoe. But their Italian beef deserves just as much respect. The best way to describe it is robust—the French loaf is stuffed with chopped, not sliced, beef, and topped with what seems to be an entire jar of giardiniera. It adds to the heft, and provides a welcome crunchy counterpoint. There’s no seating in the store itself, so the best method is to eat tailgate-style in the parking lot. Just try not to spill your food (including the fries and soda that come with everything) all over the trunk of your new car.
perfect_for_tags: Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Fast Food

review: Hiding in the most unlikely of places (in the food court at Navy Pier, stay with us) is Ciccio, a very good stall with an Italian beef unlike any other. The beef is great, the peppers are solid, but there are no dipped or wet options here. There’s only dry, or “in a bath” with slices of garlic taking a soak and a handful of tasty potatoes adding "vibes" like a funemployed friend. Ciccio’s sandwich comes on sturdy bread approximating a mini baguette, and is semi-submerged in a plastic sandwich container. If you can manage to eat this without a fork and knife, we salute you.
perfect_for_tags: Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Fast Food

review: Don't let the restaurant's name and long sections of Chinese, Japanese, and Thai dishes on the menu throw you off: Come here for the best al pastor tacos in Chicago. Yes, you read that right. As soon as you walk into the small casual spot in Little Village you’ll see the staff expertly carving a massive trompo of pork rotating around a live fire. The paper-thin slices of al pastor have the perfect balance of crispy exterior and buttery fat—all complemented by fresh green onion and sweet grilled pineapple. And though it's not officially on the menu, ask for some al pastor fried rice.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, Lunch, Quick Eats, Cheap Eats, Walk-Ins, Mexican, Chinese

review: Velvet couches, floor-to-ceiling curtains, a large golden sign above the glowing bar—The Pearl Club looks like a cocktail lounge in the height of the Roaring Twenties. But instead of Louis Armstrong, there's an upbeat electronic playlist blasting through the speakers. The first floor is spacious, but there’s an intimate loft area where you can hang out surrounded by artwork in vintage gold frames. The drink menu has solid standard cocktails and signature ones, like a nutty clarified ube colada. Plus, you can snack on things like tartare, sliders, or chicken nuggets.
perfect_for_tags: Drinking Good Cocktails, Date Night, Drinks & A Light Bite, Bar

review: At first glance, Real Thai’s menu seems to just be a line-up of the usual suspects. And while the pad thai at this relaxed Norridge restaurant is delicious, you should turn your attention to the section on their menu labeled “Secret Thai Style.” It’s full of their best dishes: fried boiled eggs in tamarind sauce, crispy mussel pancakes with chili sauce, and a Northern Thai classic: warm jackfruit salad with fresh cucumber and crispy pork skin.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Walk-Ins, Thai
full_address: 7419 W Irving Park Rd, Chicago, IL 60634

review: Starting a meal at this Edgewater spot without an order of kanom buang should be at least a misdemeanor, if not a felony. The delicate crepe is perfectly crispy and stuffed with shrimp, tofu, and coconut flakes. Follow up with the kao soi and make sure to get mango sticky rice topped with coconut milk for dessert. There, we just planned your dinner—no need to thank us. Jin Thai normally isn't busy. You’re never met with a long wait—just good Thai food and some comfy booths with squishy throw pillows.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Lunch, Walk-Ins, Thai

review: Though Siam Noodle And Rice moved in 2017 from its longtime corner spot on Sheridan to an unassuming Buena Park strip mall, this 40-year-old BYOB spot has kept its loyal following. So chances are, some of the people in their busy dining room have probably been eating their panang curry or pad prik khing with crispy pork since before the age of the iPhone. But regardless of what appetizers or entrees you get, dessert is a must—specifically their housemade coconut ice cream. It’s sweet and nutty, has a hint of salt, peanut topping, and it comes on a bed of sticky rice.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Walk-Ins, BYOB, Serious Take-Out Operation, Thai

review: With its LED light fixtures, minimalist wooden tables, and grass wall accents, Noble Thai feels a little bit like a co-working space. But chances are a WeWork membership doesn’t come with great kao soi and shredded papaya salad. And though it opened in 2021, most of the recipes at this Noble Square spot have actually been around for decades. The chef was originally a part of Chicago staple, Opart Thai, and she’s brought over some of her signature dishes like tiger cry. With lots of long tables it’s great for large groups, but it's also possible to grab a seat at their greenhouse-esque bar with a skylight for a solo meal of pad thai, a cocktail, and some sunshine.
perfect_for_tags: Big Groups, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Eating At The Bar, Serious Take-Out Operation, Walk-Ins, Date Night, Thai

review: Along with being the first city to have a skyscraper and also having the ex-tallest building in the world, Chicago can claim another marvel of engineering: the vegan food at Sephardic Sisters. This counter-service Middle Eastern restaurant in Uptown is making some incredibly meaty plant-based food. Dishes like their gyro pita or their steak shawarma (both of which come with spicy housemade zhug) are so convincing you might ask for proof that no animals were involved. Plus, while you’re fully focused on a jalapeño falafel pita or grape leaves with a zesty harissa sauce, you won’t even notice (or care about) the bare walls and complete lack of decor.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Quick Eats, Vegans, Vegetarians, Vegan, Vegetarian

review: This special occasion spot opened in 1987 and remains unapologetically formal—servers wear jackets and there will be a crisply ironed tablecloth on each table. Arun’s serves a nine-course tasting menu for $100, and it comes with beautifully plated dishes like khanom chine, and miang kum. They recently started serving a separate a la carte menu as well, with dishes like pad see ew and duck curry. You’ll still get the same great service and cocktails if you go a la carte, but you can also worry less about remembering to re-up your parking app.
perfect_for_tags: Thai

review: We’re not sure why we don’t visit this BYOB spot in Lakeview more often. It’s nice enough if you’re meeting someone’s parents for the first time, but not so formal that you’ll worry about who’s paying. Focus on the seafood—specifically dishes like the pad cha catfish, green curry fish ball pasta, or the choo chee curry with mussels. Though we normally come here for a sit-down dinner, they do a great job with takeout too.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, BYOB, Thai

review: There was a time when it seemed like every neighborhood had an Opart, a Thai staple that’s been around since 1983. Now there’s only one in West Town, but it’s still makes consistently great salads, noodle dishes, and dishes like curried whole fried fish. They’ll also customize your heat level from a range from one to seven. If you decide on anything above a five, we implore you, please order extra rice.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Thai

review: You're at El Rincón de Fabio for some of Chicago's best arepas. And if you decide to focus on anything else while you're here, there’s also a fluffy cachapa, and a patacon that deserves an Oscar for best performance in textures. In fact, the Venezuelan food at this charming Uptown spot is so compelling, you’ll look past any potential sensory overload. It’s easy to get overwhelmed by El Rincón’s flashing neon lights, butterfly decals, TVs playing concerts, and the variety of dishes on the long menu—including tacos, bowls, and Venezuelan snacks. Instead, just focus on the house specials and arepas. All the arepas come on thick, grilled dough and have plenty of fillings to choose from. But the standouts are the la veguera stuffed with pieces of steak, and the pabellón criollo, which is Venezuela’s national dish in arepa form. Regardless of what you order, the combination of fillings, cheeses, and homemade sauces that El Rincón has curated will distract you from thinking about the time you ended a work call with "love you." The arepas aren’t the only options capable of instigating an existential crisis. It’s possible to spend seven minutes debating the merits of forgoing the cachapa for a patacon, and whether you need a side order of tequeños (you do). But count on getting some help from the people who work at El Rincón. They’ll provide as much guidance as necessary and even throw in some tips on the best way to reheat your leftovers. FYI, an air fryer or oven is acceptable, using a microwave is blasphemy. El Rincón’s food should be eaten right away for optimum enjoyment, so our only complaint is that the small dining room (there’s just a handful of card tables and folding chairs) doesn’t always guarantee a seat. And make sure to ask for extra napkins because mess is unavoidable—whether from hastily gobbling down the cachapa, or because of the pulled pork juice running out of the serving basket. Either way, you won’t care. The food is too good and the service too friendly to be upset about anything.
food_rundown:
Chicken Empanada

Get this to share, or as part of the Venezuelan Taste sampler. It has a crispy crust and a doughy interior packed with shredded chicken. Take advantage of the squeeze bottles on each table, which are filled with a delicious housemade green hot sauce.


Tequeños

Is there anything more satisfying than cheese wrapped in dough and fried? Maybe, but we haven’t found it yet.


Pork Patacon

The patacon is a house specialty and deserves a lifetime achievement award for texture. The plantains are fried to the ideal level of crispiness, and when combined with soft shredded pork (our favorite filling), fresh slaw, and hot sauce, you have a perfect bite of food. They serve a smaller version in the sampler.


Pabellón Criollo Arepa

This is Venezuela’s national dish—pabellón criollo—as an arepa. Here, it gets layered with black beans, sweet plantains, shredded beef, sour cream, and a generous handful of queso blanco that melts with all the warm fillings.


La Veguera Arepa

This is the best arepa on the menu. The proportions are wonderfully balanced between the steak, fresh pico, chunky guasacaca, a tangy cilantro sauce we’d love to keep at our desks for a pick-me-up throughout the day.


Pork Cachapa

Another house specialty, you might mistake the sweet and savory cachapa for that Frette down comforter you’ll be able to afford when you’re 90. It’s so fluffy, you'll want to crawl in next to the tender chunks of pork and wrap yourself up in the corn pancake.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Lunch, Serious Take-Out Operation, Venezuelan

review: A Tavola in Ukrainian Village is easy to miss because it looks like a regular ol’ house. But just beyond the foyer (because it is, in fact, an old house) is an intimate Italian restaurant, decked out with thick window curtains and black and white photos. It's full of regulars who’ve been eating there for years, and don't be surprised if you see a kid blowing out birthday candles. And in the summer, you can enjoy pillowy housemade gnocchi or short rib risotto on the secluded back patio.
perfect_for_tags: Date Night, Walk-Ins, Unique Dining Experience, Dinner with the Parents, Italian

review: Annapurna, a vegetarian counter-service cafe in Rogers Park, has the best dosas on Devon, and probably in the city. The small dining space tends to fill up quickly during the weekend lunch rush, with people who clearly know that the masala dosa is light with delicately crispy edges, and stuffed with a well-spiced potato curry that isn’t just a pile of mush. Besides the dosas and other South Indian dishes like idli and vada (all of which come with a tangy sambar and spicy coconut chutney), there are Gujarati thalis, vegetable platters with things like malai kofta and bhindi masala, and delicious, if a little greasy, chole bhature. Skip the samosas and go for one of the other 9,372,505 different types of chaats.  Or grab a Thumbs Up and some cassata ice cream from Annapurna’s little grocery section, and sit on the brightly colored patio for some fun people-watching.
perfect_for_tags: Lunch, Vegans, Vegetarians, Walk-Ins, Indian

review: Himalayan Restaurant is a small, casual spot in the South Loop, with a menu that highlights food from Nepal and North India. There’s plenty to choose from, including big and flaky samosas packed with spicy potato filling, and some of the best biryani in the city outside of Devon. Many of their curries use ground cashews as a thickener, which calls for an order of delicious naan (pillowy soft with just the right amount of char) to sop up every last drop of the creamy gravy. Leftovers are inevitable, so Himalayan is a great weeknight option. And since most of their business is takeout, there’s almost always seating available in the low-key space.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Serious Take-Out Operation, Walk-Ins, Indian, Nepali

review: Superdawg is the iconic 1950’s style drive-in on the edge of the Chicago city limits in what is technically Norwood Park. What makes Superdawg so iconic? A few things. For one, the giant plastic hot dogs on top of the building that will make you think “that’s a really cute plastic hot dog couple.” It's endearing—the two giant plastic dogs are meant to represent the couple who opened Superdawg in 1948. Superdawg remains a true drive-in with carhop service. Pull up to any carport, place an order through the old-school-looking menu/speakerbox in front of you, and blast your favorite John Mellencamp song while you wait for your food. The wait staff doesn’t come out on roller skates, but they will hook a tray that carries all of your food on to the edge of your car window. Aside from the nostalgia of a drive-in and carhop service, Superdawg isn’t mailing it in on the food. The Superdawg is their take on the classic Chicago hot dog, and it’s differentiated by the slightly spicier beef and a pickled green tomato. The rest of the menu is pretty typical with some not-so-typical names. Get yourself a Superburger, Whoopercheesie, or some Superchickenmidgees if you choose, and of course no meal is complete without a shake or malt. You can go inside and grab a bite if you’re in a hurry, but the whole experience is where it’s at. Sit back, relax, and enjoy the classic atmosphere and food from the seat of your car.
food_rundown:
Superdawg

According to them, it’s not a wiener, not a frankfruter, and not a red hot - it’s a Superdawg. Served on a poppy seed bun, this 100% pure beef hot dog is a little spicier than most and topped with a green tomato, otherwise it’s the usual stuff.


Whoopercheesie

A double cheeseburger that’s all around not bad. Singular versions are offered in the form of a Superburger and Supercheesie.


Whoopskidawg

A polish sausage served on an onion roll type bun with grilled onions and a pickle. A good alternative to the Superdawg.


Shakes/Malts/Supersodas

In true drive-in style, you should probably cap your meal off with one of these. Regular shakes and malts are thick and delicious, while Supersodas are scoops of ice cream over chocolate, strawberry, or pineapple soda with whipped
cream and a cherry on top.


Superfries

Crinkle-cut fries that get the job done.
perfect_for_tags: Cheap Eats, Classic Establishment, Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, American, Hot Dogs

review: This is the newest stall in the Richland Center food court. And like a magician’s sleeve stuffed with Szechuan food instead of scarves, the variety of dishes coming out of their tiny kitchen is breathtaking. The menu is incredibly long, with dishes ranging from dan dan noodles and kung pao chicken to spicy frog and sesame balls. Everything we’ve ordered has a wonderful amount of mouthnumbing spice, and if you eat there, your spicy shrimp will be plated on an actual metal serving platter instead of a plastic dish.
perfect_for_tags: Serious Take-Out Operation, Quick Eats, Chinese
full_address: 2002 S Wentworth Ave B10, Chicago, IL 60616

review: Ethiopian Diamond is the oldest Ethiopian restaurant in Chicago. And the reason behind this Edgewater spot's long reign is simple: The food is fantastic. Like flaky sambusas, shimbra asa, and any stew made with their smoky “Diamond berbere” sauce—each bite grabs your attention until it’s all gone. The spacious dining room is relaxed, great for a catch-up dinner or a quiet date. And even on busier weekends, grabbing a table last minute is fairly easy.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Big Groups, Birthdays, Walk-Ins, Ethiopian

review: We had a good cry when Edgewater Ethiopian staple Ras Dashen closed. But luckily, Axum shortly took over the vacant space—and with it came the return of delicious stewed vegetables, meats, and injera. And their injera might be the hardest working in the business, capable of fitting 20 dishes on a $110 chef’s sampler for two. But you can still get smaller platters with just a few things, like dollops of shiro with roasted chickpeas or gored gored: lightly cooked, rare beef bathed in a spicy awaze and cognac sauce. Since this place usually isn't too busy, it's good for a spontaneous group dinner.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Big Groups, Walk-Ins, Ethiopian

review: Queen Sheba's exterior is covered in signage for all of the other businesses in Uptown’s Sun Plaza Strip Mall, so it's a bit hard to spot. But if you pay attention, you’ll find this cozy Ethiopian cafe just below the signs for a bank and nail salon. The small space only has four tables, but if can snag a seat it’s great for a relaxed breakfast of ful with scrambled eggs and French bread. And starting a morning off with spiced mashed chickpeas complemented by peppers, onions, and tomatoes is always the correct choice.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Coffee & A Light Bite, Walk-Ins, Ethiopian

review: The entrance to this laidback Uptown Ethiopian spot looks like a butcher shop—there’s a display case of raw beef, and meat hangs from hooks behind the counter like its part of Cirque Du Soleil. It’s foreshadowing: Selam specializes in raw dishes, like kitfo with clarified butter, or unseasoned beef, tere siga, served with mustard, a spicy sauce, and chili powder. But that's not to say you can't stop by to get some hot food—their spicy zil zil tibs and the whole rosemary-marinated fried tilapia are great.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Big Groups, Walk-Ins, Ethiopian

review: Awash’s spacious, boxy interior and hardwood floors make it feel a little like a wedding reception venue. This checks out, since you can reserve this Edgewater Ethiopian restaurant’s space for any event that warrants a 50-seat communal table: weddings, birthdays, or graduation parties. It's particularly convenient for the latter since it’s across from Loyola—it's common to find a handful of students here. Awash has classics like doro wot and gomen, along with spicy shrimp tibs or their delicious elebete. The garlicky pureed fava beans topped with olive oil nicely complements their tart injera.
perfect_for_tags: Vegetarians, Casual Weeknight Dinner, Big Groups, Walk-Ins, Ethiopian

review: Phyllis’ Musical Inn is a Wicker Park staple that has been around since 1954. Originally a bar and music venue dedicated to polka music, it now features all sorts of genres, from country to punk rock. Though most of the performances take place on their little indoor stage, when it gets nice outside, you can listen to music in their beer garden.
perfect_for_tags: Live Music, Drinking Good Beer, Bar

review: No relation to the brutal A24 Viking movie, this Northman is a spacious beer garden by the river. This River North spot has lots of picnic tables, a designated space for playing bags, and a covered stage area where you can order drinks and snacks like pretzels and hot dogs while enjoying some live music.
perfect_for_tags: Drinking Good Beer, Drinks & A Light Bite, Live Music, Big Groups, Bar

review: Afternoon Tea at LondonHouse skews informal. It takes place in the hotel’s lobby/bar, so while you’re delicately nibbling on a lemon lavender scone into, a Morningstar Investment Conference participant will be a few feet away from you loudly taking a meeting over Zoom. Despite the casual setting, the pastries look like an edible Art Basel exhibit. Everything comes out displayed on a geometric tiered tray that’s probably from CB2, and while the flavors can be hit-or-miss, the sweets are visually playful. You’ll also find tasty savories like a duck sausage spring roll, pea falafel, and an asparagus tart instead of the usual cucumber sandwich. Plus, little details are a nice touch—like a strawberry rosé jam instead of mixed fruit, and a white chocolate vanilla bean scone that’s not too sweet. Tea service is available daily, and weekdays will be relatively quiet, with the exception of the occasional conference-goer.
perfect_for_tags: Birthdays, Special Occasions, Unique Dining Experience, American

review: Coyotes in Pilsen is open very late, and nearly 24 hours: 9am to 4:30am every weekday, and 5am on the weekends. While a lot of decisions made that late at night (or early in the morning) are questionable, grabbing tacos here is not one of them. It’s a relatively small spot with just a few tables, but the menu is surprisingly long. Besides the excellent tacos, there are a bunch of breakfast options like huevos rancheros and chilaquiles, plus a variety of antojitos and entrees including gorditas, sopes, fajitas, enchiladas, quesadillas, and more. But the tacos are the real highlight—particularly the chorizo and al pastor. At $3.50 apiece, you can order multiple and be just as satisfied as if you downed an entire plate of carne asada with rice and beans.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Lunch, Serious Take-Out Operation, Mexican, Tacos

review: Los Comales is a family-run taqueria that’s been in Pilsen for more than three decades. It’s been so popular that there are two other locations in the city (in Little Village and Logan Square) plus a few in the suburbs. In other words, Los Comales is ostensibly a mini-chain. Yes, there’s a waitress that will take your order and deliver your food, but the fluorescent lighting, furniture, and menu displayed over the takeout register makes the whole place feel like a repurposed McDonald’s. And while some of the food may seem like it belongs at a fast food spot (see: steak torta with too much mayo and shredded iceberg lettuce), the tacos, horchata, and big tubs of giardiniera on each table definitely don’t. The tortillas here are light and small, and doubled up to withstand the filling. Our favorite is the al pastor, and everything else is hit-or-miss.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Lunch, Serious Take-Out Operation, Mexican, Tacos

review: Cecina Grill is a deceptively large, all-day spot in Pilsen with a long menu of tacos, burritos, soups, tortas, and bigger entrees—including a breakfast plate of chilaquiles that’s sure to cure even the most aggressive of hangovers. Families usually occupy the booths, but there’s plenty of other seating (including a diner-style bar) for anyone looking to enjoy some of the restaurant’s warm salsa de molcajete while watching the cinematic masterpiece that is Jurassic World, in Spanish. Unsurprisingly, cecina dishes are the specialty here and one of our favorites is the cecina taco, but the chorizo and al pastor tacos are very good too. As a bonus, this place is BYOB, and you’ll even get a free slice of cake on your birthday.
perfect_for_tags: Casual Weeknight Dinner, Lunch, Mexican, Tacos

review: One of the best ways to eat steak and eggs is in sandwich form at Bia’s Cafe Marianao in Irving Park (there's also another location in Dunning). It's out favorite thing at this counter service Cuban spot—thinly sliced, juicy, and peppery steak, and a great supporting cast of grilled onions, tomato, melted cheese, and a crackly long roll. They also have a tasty Cubano as well some delicious churros and pastelitos filled with guava and cheese. And if you need a pick-me up, feel free to get a colada, too.
perfect_for_tags: Breakfast, Cheap Eats, Coffee & A Light Bite, Dining Solo, Lunch, Quick Eats, Serious Take-Out Operation, Cuban

review: Unlike some of the other places with camouflaged entrances, Dorothy is hiding in plain sight. Despite having a bright red door right next to its Humboldt Park sister restaurant, Split Rail, it’s easy to miss. Once inside, this LGBTQ+ cocktail bar is surprisingly spacious, with giant comfy red couches and ‘70s-esque decor that makes it look like it was curated by a professional garage sale hunter. The drink menu is small with only eight rotating cocktails, including intriguing options like the Liquid Gold with carrot-infused rum, orange, turmeric, and oat milk. Be sure to also check their calendar for events like open mics, live music, and TV or movie screenings.
perfect_for_tags: Drinking Good Cocktails, Date Night, Bar

review: In the basement of The Green Door Tavern in River North you’ll find the bathrooms and shelves full of tchotchkes. But look closer and you’ll notice that one of those knick-knacks is actually a door knob—revealing the entrance to The Drifter. Antiques, an old American flag hanging above the bar, and short burlesque performances on a small stage complete the Prohibition era vibe. And when the curtains close, they double as a projection screen for what’s probably a Youtube playlist called “Fav Old Timey Burlesque Vids.” Adding to the mystique is the unique drink menu. Cocktail names are printed on individual tarot cards, each with fun names like Kimmy Gibbler Giblet (try saying that 10 times fast).
perfect_for_tags: Drinking Good Cocktails, Drinks & A Light Bite, Date Night, Bar

review: The Aviary’s basement bar, The Office, takes exclusivity to another level: you need a key to get in. Which means this clubhousey cocktail lounge decked out in leather couches and ornately framed artwork is great if you're a celebrity dodging the paparazzi or avoiding an ex after a Fulton Market run-in. But even if you’re not trying to be incognito, they’re still worth a visit. Just give your wallet a heads up beforehand—cocktails start at $25, like a gin fizz with a creamy layer of egg white and hints of thai basil and cardamom. But if the company card “accidentally” falls into your hands—well, why not give a $400 Brooklyn made with vintage 1940s whiskey a try?
perfect_for_tags: Date Night, Drinks & A Light Bite, Drinking Good Cocktails, Corporate Cards, Bar

review:
Editor's Note: Le Select has a new chef and menu since this was written. We will update this review soon. Le Select in River North is what we like to call a BCR: Big Chicago Restaurant. Not only are these spots physically big, but they also come from a chef or team that both your boss and your dog walker have heard of. Big Chicago Restaurants tend to get a lot of attention, and can be hit or miss.  And Le Select from the Boka Group is a BCR gone wrong.  Having dinner at this football field-sized French restaurant in River North is like eating in a mid-century cruise ship. It’s filled with old-school touches: The staff wear jackets and bowties, an hors d'oeuvres trolley rolls around the dining room, and white tablecloths stretch as far as the eye can see.  Underneath this bespoke veneer lurks a lack of refinement. This place is just too big to be elegant. Le Select is more like a fancy restaurant theme park than the real deal. Piped-in pop music is muffled by chattering diners. The harried staff is playing the parachute game with flapping tablecloths as they turnover 9,874 tables. Expensive dishes, like entrecote bordelaise and duck l’orange, are served with flimsy knives that seem stolen from a college dining hall, and dainty desserts in tiny cups come with big spoons that make them awkward to eat. The trolley might as well be just for show—there’s only one for the entire space, so count on getting those “hors d'oeuvres” in the middle of your meal. 
And that meal is going to be filled with inconsistencies. The steak au poivre is the platonic ideal of medium rare. But the ribeye covered in a red wine reduction and shallots turns to sawdust in your mouth. Salads are frequently overdressed, and the bottom of the pork and veal-filled tourte Alsacienne’s pastry is burned. But the tuna ravigote has an ideal balance of fat and acid—raw fish is snuggled next to a creamy caper sauce. Even when dishes are great (on a good night the duck l’orange is excellent), they’re still snoozy French classics.  Unless you really like red velvet chairs and brass accents, there are very few reasons to book a table at Le Select. For all its surface grandeur, there are no showstoppers on the menu to impress at a business dinner, and it’s too full of business dinners to come here for a sexy date night. Any special occasion will be overshadowed by a large group that’s three martinis deep into a loud conversation about this week’s office layoffs. If you’re looking for incredible French food downtown, you’re not going to find it at a BCR. Go to Obelix instead. It’s a bit loud, always fun, and the food never fails to impress. Oh, and it has tablecloths too.
food_rundown:
Hors D'oeuvres Cart

Hors d'oeuvres service goes for $25 per person, with things like vol au vents, and bread and a column of butter that’s carved tableside. Sounds impressive, but the rolling cart takes too long to arrive. You’re better off just ordering the $12 baguette separately.



Tuna Ravigote

This dish is the antidote to the boring crudos currently haunting Chicago menus. The sheet of raw tuna has a generous sprinkling of salt and olive oil, and is served alongside a caper-studded sauce.



Beef Tartare

Our objection with the beef tartare is that it comes with flimsy potato chips that are identical to Lays and do not have the fortitude to hold up to the wet pile of meat. The flavors are good, just plan on eating it with your fork.



Tourte Alsacienne

The Great British Bake Off has seared the horrors of a “soggy bottom” into the collective consciousness. But this savory veal and pork-filled pie overcorrects. The pastry has a tough, burnt bottom that’s hidden by a pool of mustard vinaigrette. 



Entrecôte Bordelaise

Despite being covered in a red wine sauce, the ribeye is dry. So dry, in fact, we used it as a dehumidifier. True story.



Duck Breast L’Orange

With crispy skin and tender meat, the duck l’orange is a classic dish done right. The syrupy orange sauce comes in a little pitcher, so you can control the amount like the duck breast is an IHOP pancake.



Desserts

Each dessert seems fresh out of a cooler when it arrives at the table. The coupe mont blanc and the coupe foret noir are in cold little cups, and pastry-based things like the gold leaf-covered giant eclair are stale. The icing falls off in sheets as you take a bite.
perfect_for_tags: Corporate Cards, French

review: Tea service at The Langham feels formal, and is the type someone’s great-aunt who has thoughts on “proper decorum” might like. They offer whimsical-themed teas, like an Alice In Wonderland one that involves cutely named dishes and a shot of tea to start your experience à la Alice’s “drink me” potion. But the harpist in the corner and modern furniture and art installations undercut any sense of playfulness. The food is hit-or-miss—some savory snacks like the chicken salad in a croissant are tasty, while others, like the ricotta toast, are flavorless and  messy to eat. Similarly, the scones (which arrive at the end with the rest of the sweets) have a crumbly, sand-like texture that even jam can’t help. At $115 per person, there are better options for afternoon tea in Chicago.
perfect_for_tags: Birthdays, Special Occasions, Unique Dining Experience, American

resto_name: Palm Court at The Drake Hotel
review: The Drake Hotel is the epitome of old Chicago glamour, and having afternoon tea there is like being a cast member of the Real Housewives of Gold Coast. While the Palm Court (where tea is served) is a beautiful space, it feels dated versus opulent. Yes, there’s a massive water feature in the middle of the room, and stone statues and pillars—along with hundreds of flowers—but all that decor feels like a distraction from uninspired food. The savories are like the type of mini-sandwiches you get from in-house catering at corporate events. And the sweets alternate between dry or greasy, with misshapen scones, generic chocolate madeleines, and little effort given to presentation. But it’s easy to overlook the flaws of the experience because of this spot’s history, great tea selection, and excellent service.
perfect_for_tags: Birthdays, Special Occasions, Unique Dining Experience, American

review: Tea at The Peninsula is everything you expect it to be. Assuming that you expect this fancy hotel to have soaring ceilings, impeccable service, a duo of cello players playing the theme from Pirates of the Caribbean, and a glass of Tattinger included with your meal. The tea selection is excellent, the pastries and cakes are great, and a chocolate cupcake is waiting for you as a parting gift. This experience is a great option for a special occasion, or if you just want to dress up and try one of the best afternoon teas Chicago has to offer. A couple of things to keep in mind: It’s usually booked up weeks in advance (only two seatings per weekend day) with prepaid reservations, and at $135 per person, this is one of the more expensive options in the city.
perfect_for_tags: Birthdays, Special Occasions, Unique Dining Experience, American

review: The Ritz-Carlton is the best place to have a relaxed afternoon tea in Chicago. The surroundings are relatively casual, located on the top floor of the hotel adjacent to the lobby and alongside a Starbucks (which, fortunately, is closed on Saturday and Sunday when tea service is available). Instead of dealing with tourists, you’ll be treated to a calm space with skylights, big windows, and exceptionally deep chairs you can sink into while enjoying creative snacks—like a lobster roll stuffed into a cannoli shell or a lemon buttermilk tart decorated like a baby chick. Presentation is important here, from the artfully designed food to the attentive but not intrusive service. Despite not having a large tea selection (only six options to choose from), the Ritz is one of our favorite spots for tea.
perfect_for_tags: Birthdays, Special Occasions, Unique Dining Experience, American

review: “No-frills” is the best way to sum up afternoon tea at Michigan Avenue staple Russian Tea Time. There’s no formality or pretension here, just a casual restaurant that happens to offer tea service from 11am until 7:30pm daily. For $36, you’ll get the basic tea service that includes one type of tea, some crackers with various toppings, and a few small desserts that may or may not have been purchased from Costco. Afternoon tea here feels less like a meal and more like a snack option for tourists when they need to kill time before heading to the Art Institute across the street.
perfect_for_tags: Unique Dining Experience, Pre-Theater Eats, Russian

review: Bar Pendry’s afternoon tea service is the type of spot you reserve for a bachelorette party with your friend from college who yells “Woo!" Their Sunday High Tea (which includes a boozy option) is full of groups enjoying champagne at 11am, a DJ spinning (sometimes very loud) music, and a crowd of tourists constantly walking by the windows. The space is small, and right off the lobby of the hotel on the main floor. All this can lead to more chaos than you might normally expect during afternoon tea, but the food, unique tea-based cocktails, and the crackling fireplace are worth checking out for a celebration with your most noise-tolerant friends and family.
perfect_for_tags: Birthdays, Special Occasions, Unique Dining Experience, American

review: Despite being a small restaurant tucked away in an Albany Park strip mall, Subo’s menu is huge. With over 20 entrees, plus empanadas, multiple types of egg rolls, and lots of desserts, it’s a comprehensive survey of Filipino food. They have everything from garlic rice breakfast bowls with eggs, to classics like sinigang or “chocolate meat”, a.k.a. dinuguan. This comforting pork blood stew is cooked with vinegar and different pork cuts, and gets its nickname from its rich dark color that's reminiscent of melted Hershey’s bar. But the best part about Subo is their combo rice plates that let you try a couple of dishes without needing an entourage to help you make your way through their long menu. Though if you do bring a lot of people, their $15 mountain of pancit is an incredible deal.
perfect_for_tags: Lunch, Quick Eats, Filipino

review: Our first visit to Boonie’s Filipino Restaurant was at Revival Food Hall, and we became instant fans of the pop-up-turned-food stall. We declared their sisig one of the best things we ate in 2021, and finally had a reason to tolerate the Loop. But they've since moved to a brick-and-mortar in North Center, and this iteration of Boonie’s is even better than the last. It serves incredible Filipino food in a charming space, and you’ll want to take everyone here. Even without experiencing the original Boonie’s, you can appreciate not having to eat sisig out of styrofoam in an echoey food court. Now you're eating that life-changing pork hash on a sleek cast iron plate in an equally sleek, tastefully decorated restaurant. Unlike spots that seem designed using a “Sterile Minimalist Restaurant” starter pack, Boonie's is full of unique, personality-infused touches. Framed childhood photos. Cute illustrations of cane vinegar and banana ketchup bottles. A large wooden spoon and fork hanging in the front. The music is a varied playlist of Filipino oldies, K hip-hop, and Paramore. Combine all of the above with a friendly staff that’ll boost your ego by verifying that your decision to order garlic rice with the longanisa was a smart one, and it’s easy to see why everyone in the packed dining room seems to be having a great time.  Their one-page menu—featuring a portrait of the owner’s grandma (who Boonie’s is named after)—is short and sweet. It’s divided into four sections with only a few dishes each, plus some sides like garlic rice and pickled papaya. Everything is meant to be shared and many are small plates, so don’t be surprised if you order most of the menu. The beloved spicy and citrusy sisig makes a triumphant return as a starter on the panimula section, served piping hot with a fresh egg. The inihaw portion has grilled bites like the sugpo—tender Skull Island prawn covered in an umami-loaded bagoong butter that complements the sweetness of the meat. And then there’s the sinigang: pieces of trout in a tamarind and burnt tomato broth that’s perfect for drizzling over the rice, which comes with all the larger ulam dishes.  Right by the entrance is a bright neon sign that reads “Kain Tayo,” a Tagalog saying that means “let’s eat” and is an invitation that’s especially common at parties. It perfectly embodies the communal excitement of being here, whether you’re celebrating a birthday, or just celebrating being reunited with the world's best sisig. Boonie’s has solidified itself not only as a great Filipino spot, but as one of the city’s best restaurants.
food_rundown:
Sizzling Sisig

If the sight of this sizzling plate topped with a fresh egg doesn’t hypnotize you, the seductive aroma of sauteed onions, calamansi, and crispy pork will. The egg cooks as the staff folds it into the pork hash along with a secret sauce, and the result is a combination of meaty, spicy, and tangy flavors. This is the best way to start a meal at Boonie’s.


Pancit Canton

Of the three vegetarian dishes on the menu, the pancit is the best. The stir-fried noodles are nice and chewy, and meaty mushrooms give the dish plenty of umami. But if you’re like us and want to throw some meat into the mix,  ask to top it with crispy pieces of fried pork belly.


Sugpo

This meaty Skull Island prawn is savory and slightly sweet, with a pleasant smokiness from the grill. But the generous spread of butter infused with bagoong, a popular Filipino condiment of fermented shrimp or fish paste, is what makes this dish.
